summary.title: Keep a Changelog
summary.one_liner: Learn the conventions for writing a useful changelog: curated, human-readable notable changes per version, grouped by type, with an Unreleased section and ISO 8601 dates.
keywords: changelog types added changed deprecated removed fixed security
takeaways: A changelog should be a curated, chronologically ordered list of notable changes for each version, written for humans rather than machines.
Group changes under Added, Changed, Deprecated, Removed, Fixed and Security, and keep an Unreleased section at the top.
Use ISO 8601 dates (YYYY-MM-DD) and list the latest version first.
Do not use raw git commit logs as a changelog; they are noisy. Always list deprecations, removals and breaking changes.
Show yanked releases with a [YANKED] tag rather than deleting them from the changelog.
summary.summary: This is the Keep a Changelog project page, which is itself a CHANGELOG.md file that documents the convention's own version history (from 0.0.1 in 2014 to 1.0.0 in 2017). The main body is a guide covering what a changelog is, guiding principles, the standard change types, how to maintain an Unreleased section, and why commit log diffs, ignored deprecations and ambiguous dates make changelogs bad. An FAQ compares the convention with GitHub Releases, discusses file naming, automated parsing, yanked releases and rewriting old changelogs. The page is a prescriptive opinion piece with examples rather than a tool tutorial.
